title: Beyond the Decoding Ceiling
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt argues that the difference between schools where reading feels like a gift and those where it feels like a chore comes down to positioning, not resources or timetabling. Where reading is squeezed into catch-up slots and intervention programmes, pupils absorb the message that it is remedial. Where it sits at the heart of curriculum thinking, it becomes the main way pupils meet language they could not yet reach alone. She holds that a joyful reading culture comes from the texts placed in children's hands every day, and that those choices signal what adults believe children can handle. Decoding support matters for struggling readers, but current decoding proficiency must never cap the richness of the ideas they meet, which is why reading rich texts aloud is so valuable. The practical challenge is selection: knowing what makes a text rich, resisting comprehension worksheets on first encounter, and reviewing the whole reading diet across a key stage.
points: Where reading sits in the school, as the heart of the curriculum or as a remedial add-on, shapes pupils' attitude to it more than resources do.
A pupil's decoding level should never set the ceiling on the ideas, humour and beauty of the texts they are given.
Reading rich texts aloud gives every child access to substantial ideas and phrasing they are ready to think about but cannot yet decode.
Resist cluttering the first encounter with a text with comprehension worksheets, and audit the whole reading diet across a key stage.
quotes: In some classrooms, reading is squeezed to the margins as a catch-up slot or an intervention programme, something we fit in when the real work is done. Pupils notice that quickly.

In other schools, reading sits right at the heart of curriculum thinking. It is not treated as an initiative or an add-on, but as the primary way pupils encounter language they could not yet access independently.

A joyful reading culture is not built on one-off events or laminated slogans. It is built on the texts we put into children’s hands every day, and what those choices say about what we believe they can handle.

If we say every child deserves an ambitious curriculum, our text choices have to reflect that ambition. That means offering books with humour, beauty, and difficulty, rather than thinning texts down out of caution.
Decoding support is essential for pupils who find reading tough, but their current decoding proficiency should never become a ceiling on their intellectual experience.
When we read rich texts aloud, we offer every child access to substantial ideas, beautiful phrasing, and concepts they are entirely ready to think about.

The challenge is often in the selection: knowing what makes a text rich, resisting the temptation to clutter the first encounter with comprehension worksheets, and looking at the whole reading diet across a key stage so pupils meet language that stretches them.
